title: A Calgary police officer is in a stable condition and a suspect is dead after an incident in Abbeydale
subtitle: It\'s the first shooting of an on-duty Calgary officer in about 25 years, except for a fatal training incident in 2001
article: A police constable is recovering in hospital after a gun battle Tuesday with a robbery suspect, who was later found dead in a burned out garage.
It\'s the first shooting of an on-duty Calgary officer in about 25 years, except for a fatal training incident in 2001.
Postmedia has learned the injured officer is Jordan Forget, a five-year member of the Calgary Police Service.
Officers were called to the 100 block of Abingdon Way N.E. on Tuesday morning for reports of a person trying to break into an Abbeydale home.
At a news conference Tuesday afternoon, police Chief Roger Chaffin said the incident came shortly after an armed robbery at a nearby convenience store and an attempted carjacking.
Officers flooded the area and started a massive search for the gunman, with help from the HAWCS police helicopter overhead.
The suspect opened fire on police in a confrontation between two houses. Police officers returned shots. Forget was injured in the gun battle.
The suspect was later found dead in a garage after it was set on fire. Investigators removed his body at about 6:30 p.m. for an autopsy at the medical examiner\'s office.
Chaffin said he visited Forget and the officer\'s family in hospital.

"To a great extent, he\'s very fortunate, but he\'s in good condition," Chaffin said, adding he had the support of the police force and of the officer\'s family. "They\'re there for him, he\'s getting all the support in the world, so I think he\'s doing as well as can be expected."

Roads around the scene of the incident were blocked off. Police had given orders for residents in the community to "shelter in place," which was lifted Tuesday afternoon, and Calgary police say they were not looking for any other suspects.
The Alberta Serious Incident Response Team, the province\'s independent police watchdog agency, will be investigating the shooting.
Chaffin said police still "know very little at this time" about the suspect and more details will be made public by ASIRT, which investigates all police-involved shooting.
Chaffin said police at the scene acted with "incredible courage" during the incident, adding officers are being confronted by criminals possessing firearms on an "all-too-frequent basis."
"To say I\'m proud of our members and grateful that our officer is recovering is an understatement," he said.
He also gave his thanks to members of the Calgary fire department, EMS first responders, and staff at the Foothills Medical Centre, calling them all "heroes."

"Our officers go to these scenes without a lot of information," Chaffin said. "They don\'t know what they\'re going to confront in these situations, but they use their training and their tactics and their support for each other to make sure they can be safe."
Chaffin said this incident is the first time in about 25 years he can recall an officer being shot on duty, other than in a training incident where an officer was killed in 2001.
Bernard Baker, who lives across the street from where the shooting took place, said he heard shots fired, ran to the door and saw an officer dragging a injured comrade.
"He was shot, he fell down to the ground," he said. "It was pretty stunning."
Kevin VanBroeck has lived in Abbeydale for about 20 years directly across the alley from where the garage burned down.
He said there has been at least one house fire on the block in recent years but nothing like the shooting on Tuesday.
VanBroeck didn\'t hear any gunshots and said he didn\'t realize there was an ongoing incident until he tried to leave his house and officers told him there had been a shooting in the neighbourhood.
He added he was concerned about the condition of the injured officer, and also worried the fire and smoke from the garage would cause damage to neighbouring homes.

Chaffin said members in the community may have compromised the scene "to some extent" by sharing details of the incident on social media, reminding Calgarians to be careful of what they post during a police incident.

"And these are real opportunities for harm," he said. "We have an active shooter, we have officers injured, and as images are going out, tweets are going out, compromising perhaps tactical positions ... I think all evolving communities need to understand there are times to broadcast things on social media but there are times not to."
Lisa Silver, vice-chair of the Calgary police commission, described the incident as one of the toughest situations a police officer can face.

"Every time we speak about the police, we recognize the fact that they put their lives on the line every day when they go out on their duty," she said at the beginning of a scheduled police commission meeting Tuesday, from which police members were excused.
"And today, unfortunately, it seems to be a reality. It\'s not just words that we speak. We are, however, relieved to hear that the officer is in hospital and in stable condition."

While Calgary police have been under public scrutiny for the high number of officer-involved shootings in recent years, Chaffin said there is "no such thing as a normal call" for officers, reminding the public that officers only use deadly force when their own lives are being threatened.
"It\'s just a good reminder for all of us to get that policing is a very sober and important aspect of community life, but there are certainly danger points to it," he said.
